title: Activating thermally charged quantum batteries in finite time: Thermodynamic trade-offs between correlations, work, and information
authors: Bhaskar Barman, Janine Splettstoesser, Henning Kirchberg
abstract: Thermally charged quantum batteries provide a stable and easy-to-have energy resource, but remain passive and therefore do not allow useful energy extraction on demand via unitary operations. We introduce a time-dependent stirring protocol that activates a thermally charged quantum battery through a time-dependent coupling to an auxiliary activator, thereby generating correlations that drive the battery into an active state. Accounting explicitly for the energetic cost of the stirring process, the entropic cost of correlation generation and the activation time, we derive bounds on the maximal net extractable energy. Incorporating projective measurement on the activator and exploiting the information gained through the measurement further enhances the extractable energy. As an experimentally relevant example, we analyze a waveguide-QED setup where a harmonic-oscillator battery (waveguide) is stirred and monitored by a two-level system. We characterize the performance of the protocol in terms of net extractable energy (net ergotropy) and power output.
summary: The paper proposes a protocol using time-dependent coupling (stirring) to activate passive quantum batteries, allowing for controlled energy extraction. It rigorously analyzes the thermodynamic trade-offs between work input, correlation generation, and information gain during this activation process. The results provide quantitative bounds on the maximum usable energy extractable from such systems.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a method to activate passive, thermally charged quantum batteries into an active state to enable controlled energy extraction.
main_result: The authors derive bounds on the maximal net extractable energy by explicitly accounting for the energetic cost of stirring, the entropic cost of correlation generation, and the activation time.
method: The analysis uses thermodynamic principles, quantifying useful work via ergotropy and deriving upper bounds by relating it to non-equilibrium free energy differences.
model_or_system: The model consists of a quantum battery ($\hat{H}_B$) and an ancillary activator ($\hat{H}_A$), coupled by a time-dependent interaction Hamiltonian $\hat{V}_I(t)$ during a 'stirring protocol.'
key_observables: Net extractable energy (net ergotropy), power output, work exchanged ($W_{	ext{stir}}$), and correlation build-up.
important_parameters: Activation Time ($	au$), relative temperatures ($T_A/T_B$), and frequency ratios ($\omega_A/\omega_B$).
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes that environmental effects can be neglected during the short stirring time (timescale separation), and initial states are thermal Gibbs states.
figures_summary: Figure 7 illustrates three thermodynamic operating regimes (Heat Valve, Heat Engine, Refrigerator) defined by mathematical conditions on temperatures and frequencies, showing how ergotropy varies across these regimes.
paper_structure: The paper follows a logical progression: defining the passive battery state $ightarrow$ introducing the time-dependent stirring protocol ($\hat{V}_I(t)$) $ightarrow$ deriving bounds for net extractable energy by accounting for costs $ightarrow$ applying this framework to an experimentally relevant waveguide-QED setup.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium thermodynamics and quantum resource theory, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems, quantum heat engines, and understanding energy flow in complex quantum devices.
